tacrolimus.line: Hold it and call. A magnesium this low has already stretched the QT before this drug arrives
tacrolimus.why: Magnesium stabilises the electrical reset between beats, so a low level lengthens the QT on its own. Correcting it is the half that actually lowers the torsades de pointes (a lethal twisting ventricular rhythm) risk; holding the drug while the magnesium stays this low has not made the patient safer.
tacrolimus.source: the qt rule, reasoned across parameters

tacrolimus.line: Hold it and call, AND correct the potassium and magnesium, because that is the half that actually lowers the risk
tacrolimus.why: Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what repolarizes the ventricle, and these drugs block that channel so repolarization drags out. A beat firing during that stretched window is what tips the rhythm into torsades. Holding the drug while the potassium and magnesium stay low has not made the patient safer. ⚠ Ondansetron is a QT drug: for nausea in this patient, ask for something else.

tacrolimus.line: Check a QTc first. A low calcium lengthens it, which is the part of hypocalcemia nobody expects
tacrolimus.why: Calcium is what sustains the plateau phase of the heart's electrical cycle, so a low level stretches the reset and lengthens the QT. It is the mirror image of hypercalcemia, which SHORTENS it. Correcting the calcium is what shortens the QT back.
tacrolimus.source: the qt rule, reasoned across parameters

tacrolimus.line: A different mechanism from the steroid, and it does not reverse when a dose is held
tacrolimus.why: A calcineurin inhibitor is directly toxic to the pancreatic beta cell and cuts insulin SECRETION, where a steroid causes insulin RESISTANCE. So the rise tracks the drug level rather than the dose timing, it does not come back down the way steroid hyperglycemia does, and post-transplant diabetes is a real long-term outcome rather than a passing number.

tacrolimus.line: Check a QTc before giving it, because the low potassium has already lengthened it
tacrolimus.why: Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what repolarizes the ventricle. At this level that is already impaired, so a QT drug lands on a QT that is long before the drug arrives. Correcting the potassium is what lowers the risk; holding the drug alone does not.
tacrolimus.source: the qt rule, reasoned across parameters

tacrolimus.line: Not a sodium issue directly. Check the potassium and magnesium, which usually fell with it
tacrolimus.why: Hyponatremia from a thiazide rarely arrives alone, and it is the potassium and magnesium that lengthen the QT. The sodium is what explains the confusion; the other two are what change your QT risk.
tacrolimus.source: the qt rule, reasoned across parameters

also.line: Check how each one is cleared, because several of these are renally dosed
also.why: Levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin both need dose reduction in reduced kidney function, and an accumulated fluoroquinolone brings both QT prolongation and a lower seizure threshold with it.
also.source: the qt rule, reasoned across parameters

acetaminophen.line: The 4 g ceiling is for a HEALTHY liver. Total every source first, and expect a lower limit here
acetaminophen.why: Acetaminophen is cleared by two safe routes that have a ceiling. Past it, a backup enzyme makes a toxic by-product that kills liver cells, and the thing that neutralises it runs out. In liver disease, in a chronic alcohol user, or in malnutrition, that reserve is already low, so the ceiling drops, often to 2 g a day or less. The real danger is arithmetic: APAP hides in combination cough and cold products, in oxycodone-acetaminophen, in Percocet, and patients do not count it as a drug. ⚠ Early toxicity looks like nothing at all, which is why the ceiling is the control rather than the symptoms.

celecoxib.line: Stop it and say why. This is the commonest reversible cause of a BP that was controlled and is not
celecoxib.why: NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that dilate vessels and help the kidney excrete sodium, so the antihypertensive works less well AND sodium is retained. Nine days of ibuprofen is exactly the timeline. If a question hands you a patient whose controlled pressure suddenly is not, look for a new over-the-counter NSAID before you look for nonadherence.

celecoxib.line: STOP IT. Of everything on this list, the NSAID is the easiest thing to remove and the most worth removing
celecoxib.why: Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole, the vessel carrying blood INTO the glomerulus. An NSAID blocks them, so the inlet narrows at the moment perfusion depends on it staying open. Combined with an ACE inhibitor relaxing the outlet and a diuretic dropping the volume arriving at both, that is the triple whammy, and it is one of the commonest preventable causes of hospital-acquired kidney injury.

celecoxib.line: Not the pressure problem here. It is the kidney problem
celecoxib.why: An NSAID raises blood pressure, so it is not lowering this one. What it does at this pressure systolic is narrow the afferent arteriole at the moment renal perfusion depends on it staying open, which is how a low pressure becomes an acute kidney injury.
celecoxib.source: the bp_blunting rule, with the verdict written down rather than derived

codeine.line: Hold it and call. Magnesium is already depressing her breathing, and an opioid on top is how it stops
codeine.why: The magnesium label names narcotics specifically, for potentiated and prolonged CNS depression. At this level with an absent reflex and a respiratory rate of 11, the next dose of anything sedating lands on a patient whose reserve has already gone.
codeine.source: the cns_resp rule, reasoned across parameters

codeine.line: Give it for real pain, at a reduced dose, and check the pressure after
codeine.why: Opioids release histamine and reduce vascular tone, so the pressure falls, and it falls furthest in a patient who is volume depleted or sitting up. Taken with the sedation, that is how an ordinary dose becomes a fall. Pain is a real indication and this is not a reason to leave her in it.
codeine.source: the cns_resp rule, reasoned across parameters

codeine.line: Only methadone, and it is the one to know
codeine.why: Methadone prolongs the QT and the effect rises with the level, so an ECG that was acceptable at the start can drift as the dose is titrated or as an interacting drug slows its clearance. The other opioids are not QT drugs.
codeine.source: the cns_resp rule, reasoned across parameters

naproxen.line: Stop it and say why. This is the commonest reversible cause of a BP that was controlled and is not
naproxen.why: NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that dilate vessels and help the kidney excrete sodium, so the antihypertensive works less well AND sodium is retained. Nine days of ibuprofen is exactly the timeline. If a question hands you a patient whose controlled pressure suddenly is not, look for a new over-the-counter NSAID before you look for nonadherence.

naproxen.line: STOP IT. Of everything on this list, the NSAID is the easiest thing to remove and the most worth removing
naproxen.why: Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole, the vessel carrying blood INTO the glomerulus. An NSAID blocks them, so the inlet narrows at the moment perfusion depends on it staying open. Combined with an ACE inhibitor relaxing the outlet and a diuretic dropping the volume arriving at both, that is the triple whammy, and it is one of the commonest preventable causes of hospital-acquired kidney injury.

naproxen.line: Not the pressure problem here. It is the kidney problem

lithium.line: HOLD IT AND CALL for a level. A sodium this low means a lithium level from yesterday is already wrong
lithium.why: The kidney handles lithium exactly like sodium. When sodium falls, the proximal tubule reabsorbs more of both, so the lithium level climbs with no change in dose. A level of 0.8 drawn before the sodium fell tells you nothing about now. FINE tremor is expected on lithium; COARSE tremor, ataxia and slurred speech are toxicity.

lithium.line: The opposite direction, and it costs you effect rather than safety
lithium.why: When sodium is high the kidney reabsorbs less lithium, so the level FALLS and the patient can relapse on an unchanged dose. The general rule is the useful one: any change in sodium or hydration in a lithium patient means rechecking the level, in either direction.

methylphenidate.line: Hold it and call. It raises the rate directly
methylphenidate.why: Methylphenidate raises synaptic norepinephrine, so rate and pressure both climb. In a patient at this rate it is removing the ceiling.
methylphenidate.source: the stimulant_bp rule, reasoned across parameters

magnesium-sulfate.line: STOP THE INFUSION AND CALL. Have calcium gluconate ready, because that is the antidote
magnesium-sulfate.why: The infusion is the source, so stopping it IS the treatment, and calcium gluconate buys time by opposing magnesium at the neuromuscular junction. Read the findings in order: the deep tendon reflex goes FIRST, then the respiratory rate, then the heart. An absent patellar reflex is not an early sign, it is the one you already passed.

magnesium-sulfate.line: IV magnesium is what actually fixes a potassium that will not come up
magnesium-sulfate.why: Low magnesium makes the distal nephron waste potassium, so replacement runs out as fast as it goes in. Correct the magnesium first, or alongside. Watch the patellar reflex and the respiratory rate while it infuses.

magnesium-sulfate.line: This is the treatment, and replacing it is what finally lets the potassium come up
magnesium-sulfate.why: Low magnesium makes the distal nephron waste potassium, so potassium replacement runs out as fast as it goes in. Correct the magnesium first, or alongside. Watch the patellar reflex and the respiratory rate while it infuses, because the reflex goes before the breathing does.

magnesium-sulfate.line: IV magnesium is the treatment for torsades, and it works whether or not the magnesium is low
magnesium-sulfate.why: In torsades de pointes, magnesium suppresses the triggered beats that start it, which is why it is given on the rhythm rather than on the level. In this patient it does both jobs at once: her magnesium of 1.1 is part of why the QT is 512. Watch the patellar reflex and the respiratory rate, because the reflex goes first.

oxytocin.line: Watch the total volume, because oxytocin has an antidiuretic effect of its own
oxytocin.why: At high doses in a large volume of hypotonic fluid it causes water intoxication, with seizures as the endpoint. The fix is attention to the infusion volume and the fluid it is mixed in, not a different drug.

azithromycin.line: Hold it and call. A magnesium this low has already stretched the QT before this drug arrives
azithromycin.why: Magnesium stabilises the electrical reset between beats, so a low level lengthens the QT on its own. Correcting it is the half that actually lowers the torsades de pointes (a lethal twisting ventricular rhythm) risk; holding the drug while the magnesium stays this low has not made the patient safer.
azithromycin.source: the qt rule, reasoned across parameters

azithromycin.line: Hold it and call, AND correct the potassium and magnesium, because that is the half that actually lowers the risk
azithromycin.why: Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what repolarizes the ventricle, and these drugs block that channel so repolarization drags out. A beat firing during that stretched window is what tips the rhythm into torsades. Holding the drug while the potassium and magnesium stay low has not made the patient safer. ⚠ Ondansetron is a QT drug: for nausea in this patient, ask for something else.

azithromycin.line: Check a QTc first. A low calcium lengthens it, which is the part of hypocalcemia nobody expects
azithromycin.why: Calcium is what sustains the plateau phase of the heart's electrical cycle, so a low level stretches the reset and lengthens the QT. It is the mirror image of hypercalcemia, which SHORTENS it. Correcting the calcium is what shortens the QT back.
azithromycin.source: the qt rule, reasoned across parameters

azithromycin.line: Check a QTc before giving it, because the low potassium has already lengthened it

azithromycin.line: Not a sodium issue directly. Check the potassium and magnesium, which usually fell with it

azithromycin.source: the qt rule, reasoned across parameters

isoniazid.line: Hold it and call. Isoniazid hepatotoxicity is the reason this drug gets monthly liver panels

Those are what the patient is taught to report, because waiting for jaundice is waiting too long. Give pyridoxine with it for the separate neuropathy risk.

cimetidine.line: Flag it and ask how long they have been on it. The PPI label names this, and almost nobody checks for it
cimetidine.why: Prolonged proton pump inhibitor therapy causes hypomagnesemia, and the label asks for a magnesium level before starting and periodically afterwards in anyone also taking digoxin or a diuretic. It takes months to years to appear, so it never looks like a new drug problem. Stopping the PPI is usually what fixes it; replacement alone does not hold while the drug continues.
cimetidine.source: the acid_dependent_absorption rule, reasoned across parameters

cimetidine.line: Contributing, and it changes which calcium SALT to use
cimetidine.why: Calcium carbonate needs stomach acid to dissolve, and a PPI or H2 blocker holds the pH up all day, so less gets absorbed and the deficiency does not correct. Calcium CITRATE does not need acid and is the better choice in anyone on acid suppression.
cimetidine.source: the acid_dependent_absorption rule, reasoned across parameters

prochlorperazine.source: the qt rule, reasoned across parameters

prochlorperazine.line: Check a QTc before giving it, because the low potassium has already lengthened it
prochlorperazine.why: Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what repolarizes the ventricle. At this level that is already impaired, so a QT drug lands on a QT that is long before the drug arrives. Correcting the potassium is what lowers the risk; holding the drug alone does not.
prochlorperazine.source: the qt rule, reasoned across parameters

prochlorperazine.line: Not a sodium issue directly. Check the potassium and magnesium, which usually fell with it
prochlorperazine.why: Hyponatremia from a thiazide rarely arrives alone, and it is the potassium and magnesium that lengthen the QT. The sodium is what explains the confusion; the other two are what change your QT risk.
prochlorperazine.source: the qt rule, reasoned across parameters

prochlorperazine.line: Check how each one is cleared, because several of these are renally dosed
prochlorperazine.why: Levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin both need dose reduction in reduced kidney function, and an accumulated fluoroquinolone brings both QT prolongation and a lower seizure threshold with it.
prochlorperazine.source: the qt rule, reasoned across parameters

promethazine.line: Hold it and call. A magnesium this low has already stretched the QT before this drug arrives
promethazine.why: Magnesium stabilises the electrical reset between beats, so a low level lengthens the QT on its own. Correcting it is the half that actually lowers the torsades de pointes (a lethal twisting ventricular rhythm) risk; holding the drug while the magnesium stays this low has not made the patient safer.
promethazine.source: the qt rule, reasoned across parameters

promethazine.line: Hold it and call, AND correct the potassium and magnesium, because that is the half that actually lowers the risk
promethazine.why: Potassium leaving the cell through the hERG channel is what repolarizes the ventricle, and these drugs block that channel so repolarization drags out. A beat firing during that stretched window is what tips the rhythm into torsades. Holding the drug while the potassium and magnesium stay low has not made the patient safer. ⚠ Ondansetron is a QT drug: for nausea in this patient, ask for something else.

promethazine.line: Reduce it or choose something else, especially IV and especially in an older adult
promethazine.why: It blocks the alpha-1 receptor, the one that tightens blood vessels, so the pressure drops, and the drop is worst after an IV dose. ⚠ It also causes severe tissue injury including gangrene by any parenteral route, and the maximum IV concentration is 1 mg/mL, not the 25 mg/mL still widely taught.

bisacodyl.line: Stop the scheduled dose and ask how long they have been taking it
bisacodyl.why: Potassium leaves in stool as well as urine, and chronic laxative use is an easily missed cause in an older adult, especially one who buys it over the counter and does not think of it as a medication.
bisacodyl.source: the hypokalemia rule, with the verdict written down rather than derived

lactulose.line: This IS the treatment for hepatic encephalopathy, and the dose endpoint is the stools
lactulose.why: Ammonia builds up when the liver cannot convert it, and it crosses into the brain. Lactulose acidifies the colon, which traps ammonia as ammonium so it leaves in the stool, and it speeds transit so there is less time to absorb. ⚠ Titrate to 2 to 3 SOFT STOOLS a day: the stools are the dose endpoint, not a side effect to suppress. Holding it because the patient has diarrhea is how someone gets worse.

magnesium-hydroxide.line: Stop it, and in kidney impairment keep it off the list permanently
magnesium-hydroxide.why: An over-the-counter antacid and laxative becomes a real drug when the kidney cannot excrete magnesium. Patients do not think of it as medication and do not report it, so ask by brand name.

magnesium-hydroxide.line: Avoid it. Magnesium accumulates when the kidney cannot excrete it
magnesium-hydroxide.why: An over-the-counter laxative and antacid becomes a real drug in kidney impairment, and magnesium toxicity presents as lost deep tendon reflexes, then respiratory depression. Choose a laxative that is not magnesium-based.

magnesium-hydroxide.line: Only worth knowing for the magnesium, and the magnesium is the point
magnesium-hydroxide.why: You cannot correct potassium while magnesium is low, because low magnesium makes the kidney waste potassium no matter how much you give. So a potassium this low that will not come up is a magnesium problem. This is an oral antacid rather than the replacement route, but the principle is what matters.

magnesium-hydroxide.line: An oral option for a mild deficiency, with a predictable side effect
magnesium-hydroxide.why: It is a laxative first and a magnesium source second, so diarrhea is the limit on how much a patient will take. For a magnesium this low with a potassium that will not correct, the IV route is the one that works.

senna.line: Stop the scheduled dose and ask how long they have been taking it
senna.why: Potassium leaves in stool as well as urine, and chronic laxative use is an easily missed cause in an older adult, especially one who buys it over the counter and does not think of it as a medication.
senna.source: the hypokalemia rule, with the verdict written down rather than derived

calcium-acetate.line: Stop it and call. The binder needs changing rather than pausing
calcium-acetate.why: It is binding phosphate, which still needs doing, so the answer is a non-calcium binder such as sevelamer rather than simply stopping. That is a provider decision, and it is the one to prompt.

calcium-acetate.line: It raises calcium, but it is prescribed to bind PHOSPHATE, so do not treat it as replacement
calcium-acetate.why: In kidney disease it is given with meals specifically to trap phosphate in the gut. Away from food it behaves as a calcium supplement. The timing is the whole difference.

calcium-acetate.line: Also a phosphate binder, not a potassium treatment, and not the calcium you are thinking of
calcium-acetate.why: The calcium that stabilizes the cardiac membrane in hyperkalemia is IV calcium gluconate or chloride, given to buy time while the shifting and removing drugs work. An ORAL calcium salt does none of that.

sevelamer.line: Not a calcium drug at all, which is exactly why it gets chosen
sevelamer.why: It binds phosphate WITHOUT adding calcium, which is the reason to pick it over a calcium-based binder in a patient whose calcium is a problem. In this patient, whose calcium is low, that is a reason to ask whether the binder choice still fits.

sevelamer.line: Not a potassium drug. It binds phosphate, and it binds most other oral drugs with it
sevelamer.why: Named because it turns up on every kidney med list next to the potassium problem and gets assumed to be part of it. Its real nursing issue is timing: other oral drugs go 1 hr before it or 3 hr after.

alendronate.line: DO NOT START IT. A low calcium is a labeled contraindication, and it has to be corrected first
alendronate.why: A bisphosphonate works by stopping bone from releasing calcium, so giving one to a patient who is already low drives the calcium lower and can produce tetany. Correct the calcium and the vitamin D first. This is also why calcium and vitamin D are prescribed ALONGSIDE a bisphosphonate rather than instead of it.

alendronate.line: A bisphosphonate IS the treatment for hypercalcemia of malignancy, which is likely what this is
alendronate.why: It stops bone from releasing calcium, which is where the calcium is coming from in a patient with metastatic disease. It takes two to four days to work, so fluids carry the first 48 hours. Note the reversal: the same drug is contraindicated when the calcium is LOW.

calcium-carbonate.line: Stop it. It is adding calcium to a level that is already this high
calcium-carbonate.why: Obvious once you look at the list, and easy to miss because patients count it as a supplement rather than a medication. Ask about antacids too, since many are calcium carbonate.

calcium-carbonate.line: Same point. An oral calcium salt is not the membrane-stabilizing treatment
calcium-carbonate.why: IV calcium is what is given for the ECG changes of hyperkalemia. Oral calcium carbonate is an antacid and a phosphate binder, and it also binds other oral drugs in the gut.

calcium-carbonate.line: This is the treatment, and the salt matters if she is on acid suppression
calcium-carbonate.why: Calcium carbonate needs stomach acid to dissolve. In a patient on a PPI or an H2 blocker, calcium CITRATE is absorbed without acid and is the better choice. Give it with vitamin D, since calcium without it is poorly absorbed.

donepezil.line: Flag it. Few people think of an antiepileptic as a rate drug
donepezil.why: Lacosamide prolongs the PR interval, so it adds to AV block in a patient already on a rate-slowing drug. It is not the cause of a rate this low on its own, and it is worth naming on a list where everything else has an obvious cardiac reason.
donepezil.source: the bradycardia rule, with the verdict written down rather than derived

mannitol.line: HOLD THE NEXT DOSE AND CALL. Above about 320 the osmolarity stops being the goal and becomes the risk
mannitol.why: Mannitol works BY raising serum osmolarity, so a climbing number means the drug is doing its job, which is what makes the ceiling easy to miss. Past roughly 320 mOsm/L the risk turns into kidney injury, and the osmolarity is the parameter that decides whether the next dose goes in. Check the osmolar GAP too, meaning the difference between the measured value and the one calculated from sodium, glucose and BUN, because that gap is the mannitol itself.

sodium-bicarbonate.line: Stop counting it as a bicarbonate and start counting it as salt. 50 mEq of sodium per amp
sodium-bicarbonate.why: One 50 mL amp of 8.4 percent carries 50 mEq of sodium, about what is in 330 mL of normal saline. Several in a code is a sodium load that never appears on an intake record as salt, and in a patient at this level who is not drinking freely it is a direct contributor.

sodium-bicarbonate.line: Give it if the glucose needs it, and recheck the potassium after, not tomorrow
sodium-bicarbonate.why: Insulin and bicarbonate do not remove potassium, they drive it INTO cells, so the serum number falls within the hour. That is the trap in a hyperglycemic patient who is also hypokalemic: treating the glucose makes the potassium worse, and both numbers need watching.
sodium-bicarbonate.source: the hypokalemia rule, with the verdict written down rather than derived

sodium-bicarbonate.line: Count it. Each amp is a sodium load, and sodium is what the osmolarity mostly measures
sodium-bicarbonate.why: One 50 mL amp of 8.4 percent carries 50 mEq of sodium. Several of them push the sodium and the osmolarity in the same direction, and it never appears on an intake record as salt.

sodium-bicarbonate.line: This is the treatment. Insulin with dextrose is the fastest way to bring it down
sodium-bicarbonate.why: Insulin drives potassium into the cell within 15 to 30 minutes, which is faster than anything that removes it. The thing to hold on to is that it SHIFTS rather than removes: total body potassium has not changed, so the number comes back up as the insulin wears off, and the real removal still has to happen. Bicarbonate shifts it too, and works best when there is an acidosis to correct.
